reader_question: How has the typical household’s income changed, and how sure is each year’s figure?
title: Median household income stood at $87,460 in 2025, in 2025 dollars, the highest since the survey’s first year, 1967.
measure_line: Median household income in 2025 dollars, each year from 1967 to 2025, United States, the whole series. The band spans each year’s 90 percent margin of error.
reading_guide: The line breaks in 2013, where new income questions put the year’s two estimates $2,200 apart. A new processing system in 2017 put them $300 apart, close enough that the two dots overlap; the table prints both.
notes: The 2025 figure carries a margin of error of plus or minus $1,040 at 90 percent confidence; its lead over 2019’s $85,320, the next highest year, and its rise over 2024’s $85,210 both pass the margin of the gap.

The figures count income before taxes, from the Current Population Survey’s Annual Social and Economic Supplement. The Bureau adjusts each year to 2025 dollars with the chained consumer price index from 2000 on, and with the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ research series of the consumer price index for the years before 2000.
alt: A line of median household income from 1967 to 2025 in 2025 dollars, with a light band, edged by thin gray lines, for each year’s margin of error. It rises from $56,230 in 1967 to $87,460 in 2025, the highest of the series, and breaks in 2013, where new survey questions put the year’s two estimates $2,200 apart. In 2017 a new processing system put them $300 apart, close enough that the two dots overlap.

chart_notes: Two thin gray lines, one above and one below the dark line, edge a light band that spans each year’s margin of error. Where a year’s margin is narrower than the line, the band hides behind it; the table gives every margin. In 2013 and 2017 the line breaks and draws both of the year’s estimates as dots; 2025 is labeled at the line’s end.
